title: Dynamic GPU clock & kernel heuristic for heterogeneous H100/L40S/A10 MIG fleets
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Goal: Reduce P99 latency and improve sustained throughput across mixed GPU fleets by combining dynamic kernel-selection heuristics with per-MIG and per-device clock/power profiles and a lightweight prefill/decode scheduler.

Background: We run heterogeneous fleets (H100, L40S, A10) with MIG partitions in several clusters. Static clocking and a one-size-fits-all kernel chooser cause suboptimal performance: small-batch low-latency traffic tends to hit the largest kernels (high-power), while long-prefill jobs trigger contention and noisy neighbors on shared MIG partitions.

Hypothesis: A runtime component that (1) selects attention kernels and compute kernels based on model shape + sequence-length histogram, (2) adjusts per-MIG power/profile for latency-sensitive partitions, and (3) prioritizes prefill work vs decode work using a windowed scheduler will yield measurable P99 latency reduction and throughput uplift without increasing cost substantially.

Design overview:
- Kernel heuristic: extend kernel-selector module to probe and maintain a small table (model-size, seq-range, batch-range) -> preferred kernel family (FlashAttention-v2, tiled-attn, fused-kernel). Probing runs in background with low-frequency synthetic runs and periodic live-sample verification.
- Clock/power profiles: define three named profiles for each device type: latency_boost (higher clocks, aggressive power), balanced (default), and throughput_cap (lower clocks to increase thermal headroom for multi-tenant). Allow profile assignment per MIG slice.
- Prefill/decode scheduler: implement a short-window scheduler that favors decode work for latency-path tokens while allowing prefill to run opportunistically if queue depth is low. Introduce a prefill priority token and a per-request deadline hint used by the scheduler.
- Routing policy: tie kernel heuristics to smart routing: small-batch low-latency requests prefer L40S slices in latency_boost profile; cheap embedding or bulk offline workloads target A10 throughput_cap slices.

Bench plan and metrics:
- Benchmarks: gpt-medium (7B), llama2-13B, and a trimmed eval set with seq lengths {64,512,2048,8192}. Test batches [1,4,16].
- Metrics: P50/P90/P99 latency, median/95 throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, MIG steal rate, tail-power spikes, and cost per 1M tokens.
- Targets: P99 reduction on latency path >= 8-12% on H100/L40S; throughput gain >= 15% for mixed long-prefill workloads.

Implementation tasks:
1) Kernel-selector extension: add probing harness, persistent table, and runtime switch. (ENG changes + small proto buffers)
2) Power profiles: add device-profile API in infra + agent that calls nvidia-smi/rocm-smi or NVML where available; safety: fallback to balanced on error.
3) Prefill/decode scheduler: runtime queue scoring, deadline hints propagation to client SDKs, and graceful starvation prevention for prefill.
4) Telemetry: add per-request kernel-choice tag, power-profile tag, queue wait time and deadline-violation counter.
5) Canary + rollout: stage on a few dedicated clusters with controlled traffic, run A/B against baseline for 72h.

Risks and mitigations:
- Clock changes can increase thermal degradation; mitigation: limit frequency of profile switches per device and require explicit operator approval for aggressive profiles.
- Probing noise could cause oscillation: use exponential backoff and moving averages.
- Multi-tenant fairness: default to balanced profile on shared partitions unless customer-level affinity is present.

Rollout plan:
- Week 1: implement kernel-selector probe logic + telemetry.
- Week 2: add device-profile agent and simple scheduler; internal canary tests on dev cluster.
- Week 3: 2-cluster canary (staging, us-east); monitor for regressions.
- Week 4: gradual rollout to production clusters with automated rollback on >5% regression in P50 or any P99 increase.

Success criteria: stable P99 improvement on latency path across canary clusters, no more than 2% increase in cost per token, and no customer-reported degradations during rollouts.
